logline: Tracey Gordon, 24, devoutly Christian and fiercely naive, decides it is time to have sex and learn how the world works - in a British housing estate comedy that announces Michaela Coel as a voice unlike any other.

renewal.note: Michaela Coel ended the series after two seasons to pursue I May Destroy You (BBC / HBO, 2020), which drew on her own experience of sexual assault.

bollymeter.basis: 100% on Rotten Tomatoes (32 reviews across both seasons); BAFTA for Best Female Comedy Performance and Best Breakthrough Talent for Michaela Coel in 2016. Critics called it one of the most original British sitcom debuts in years.

seasons.review_body: Michaela Coel wrote, created, and starred in Chewing Gum as a commission from E4, building on a stage monologue about a Jehovah's Witness girl determined to lose her virginity. The result was one of the sharpest British sitcom debuts in a generation. Season 1 holds 100% on Rotten Tomatoes. Coel's Tracey Gordon operates in a register all her own - the comedy comes from the gap between her faith-shaped innocence and a world that runs on entirely different rules, but Coel never condescends to the character or to the estate. The physical comedy is extraordinary: Tracey's fantasies, rendered literally, are timed with a precision that recalls classic Chaplin more than contemporary TV comedy. The BAFTA for Best Female Comedy Performance and Best Breakthrough Talent in 2016 confirmed what the critical response had already indicated. Watching Season 1 knowing what Coel would make next - I May Destroy You - adds retrospective weight to the tenderness underneath the jokes.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The first episode introduces Tracey, her controlling mother Shirley, boyfriend Ronald, and the housing estate that is Chewing Gum's entire world. Coel's physical comedy arrives fully formed; the first fantasy sequence establishes the show's visual grammar and its willingness to go further than any British sitcom debut had in years.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Tracey's first fantasy sequence, which turns a mundane conversation about desire into a full music-video production number that collapses back into the reality of her mother's flat.

bollymeter.basis: 100% on Rotten Tomatoes (16 reviews); critics noted Coel's writing had grown bolder and the character's emotional range had widened, even as the comedy remained sharp.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 brought a more confident Tracey and a more ambitious Coel. The comedy darkened slightly - the estate's realities pressed harder against Tracey's optimism - while the fantasy sequences grew more formally inventive. Critics remained unanimous: 100% on Rotten Tomatoes from 16 reviews, with notices pointing to the emotional complexity that had arrived underneath the outrageous set pieces. The season also deepened the supporting cast, particularly Susan Wokoma's Candice, whose friendship with Tracey became the emotional core. Coel ended the series here by choice, and the finale's combination of comedy and genuine loss marked it as a show that had said what it came to say. Netflix's international pickup brought Chewing Gum to a global audience that came to it, often, only after I May Destroy You.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 2 carries more weight without losing the comic velocity - Tracey's world has widened, and Coel's writing has grown to fill it.
